source_reviews.independent_solution: For ordinary electrolytic metal deposition, connect the metal object to the negative terminal so its surface is the cathode, and place the anode within the electrolyte-filled cavity facing the desired inner surface without electrical contact with the object. Metal ions in a suitable plating electrolyte are reduced at the cathodic inner wall. If a soluble coating-metal anode is used it can replenish those ions, but a soluble anode is not universally necessary when electrolyte supply is otherwise maintained.

source_reviews.independent_solution: In the ideal Faraday electrolysis model with the same depositing species and charge state and equal current efficiency, the same series current flows through every cell for the same time. Each therefore receives the same charge Q=It and deposits the same mass m=kQ. Different concentration can change the cell's voltage requirement or resistance, but does not give different series charges. Outside this model, differing depletion or side reactions can change useful deposition efficiency, so equal mass is not an unconditional statement for arbitrary real cells.

coverage.evidence: The same electrolyte, concentration difference and series comparison survive. Explicit authored ideal conditions are not retroactively called printed source facts. source_reviews.independent_solution: Under the ordinary steady electrolysis interpretation, positive and negative ions cross in opposite drift directions. Reversing both charge sign and drift direction makes their conventional-current contributions have the same sign, so the transported-current charge magnitude is3C+2C=5C. I=5C/1s=5A in the external circuit. Subtracting the charge magnitudes would instead confuse net signed charge with charge contributing to through-current.

source_reviews.independent_solution: Ordinary electrolyte dissociation separates dissolved electrolyte species into mobile positive and negative ions; for an ionic compound dissolution separates existing ionic constituents rather than necessarily stripping electrons into a free-electron population. Gas ionization commonly involves an energetic collision or radiation removing an electron from a neutral atom/molecule, producing a positive ion and a free electron. Subsequent attachment can also form negative gas ions. Thus neither mechanism should be defined simply as every ion losing an electron, and the liquid/gas carrier distinction does not imply that all gas ions are positive.

mathematics.independent_solution: Use the frozen source7 distinction. Solvent action can disperse electrolyte ions, while electron-loss ionization makes a positive gas ion and electron. Ionic solids may separate existing ions, molecular solutes may form ions through solvent reaction, and gas electrons may attach to create negative ions. Electrolytes are not predominantly free-electron conductors, gas current is not ions-only, and the universal pre-existing-ion claim is false. The set is a,c.
